text: So, as we take our first step towards SG100, let us make this a journey of closer partnerships.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Let us work together to build a better home with our families and a better community with our neighbours and fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Let us shape, together, our residential and urban landscape and build the best Singapore we know how for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Municipal issues may seem mundane, almost ordinary but the extra-ordinary efforts are taken to solve the problems of our citizens.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: What must really make the work of the Municipal Services Office (MSO) difficult in the last one year must be ploughing through, what I call, the three big mountains – a mountain of feedback to sort, a gunung of red tape to unravel and one bukit full of agencies to coordinate.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: While the Minister-in-charge has lauded partner agencies for the progress made by MSO, are there still challenges yet to be resolved?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Does the MSO project more for the coming year and what other feedback mechanisms are in place, especially for the elderly?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: I am also sure I am not the only one to notice the app has a minor bug that seems to make the name the Infocomm Development Authority (IDA) officer who worked on the app appear every time we load it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: I think thanks are due to this particular staff and the team for their good first effort at an all-encompassing app.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Would MSO also update on the integration of the systems with Town Councils?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Has the pilot progressed and what are the major hurdles, if any?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Would the Ministry share what have been the improvements in terms of the coordination among its partner agencies?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: One of the key initiatives by MSO was the OneService app.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: What proportion of the partner agencies' feedback comes from OneService app?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: I understand that MSO has been making enhancements to the OneService app, including adding new reporting categories.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Would the Minister share with us an overview of the enhanced features and what are the plans for the OneService app going forward?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: What other agencies will be added as partners?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Last year, the focus had been on making feedback easier for residents and working with agencies to address feedback more effectively.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Would MSO take on a further role to review partner agencies' actions on the feedback?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Would MSO provide feedback to partner agencies to improve their processes and workflow so as to improve service delivery to the public?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: With growing manpower and resource constraints, how does MSO and its partner agencies leverage technology to boost the productivity of municipal service delivery?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In the past, members of the public might not know which agency to call and get bounced around by the different agencies before action is taken.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The app was designed to make it more convenient for the public to report municipal issues in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In the follow-up to the OneService app, MSO mentioned that they will continue to fine tune and improve on the functionalities and performance of the app, taking into account public feedback and suggestions for improvements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: MSO also plans to invite more agencies to participate in the app and include additional features in future versions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can MSO now provide updates on how it will improve the app further, whether more agencies will be participating in it and what are any further plans for the OneService app going forward?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Its objective was to help provide a one-stop shop for municipal issues, such as estate cleanliness and maintenance.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: That way, residents would not need to navigate the various Government agencies in charge of different operations and services.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: It has now been slightly more than a year since the MSO was set up.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Looking back at this first year, a key initiative of the MSO was the launching of the OneService app.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: With the widespread use of mobile communication devices in Singapore, such an app should in principle help the MSO extend outreach more effectively.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: And how many requests for assistance have been received via this app?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Looking ahead, what plans does the MSO have in terms of enhancements to the OneService app?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Baey Yam Keng, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I note that the new arrangement does not include grassland under the Town Councils' responsibility.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: However, there are areas where a plot of Town Council land and another plot under NParks are side by side, for example a strip of land between Tampines Block 498 cluster and the Tampines Expressway, which does not have a clear physical boundary.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Currently, when both agencies have different schedules, there is no one time when the grass of the entire strip is nicely cut.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Apart from public greenery maintenance, there are still other municipal services today that are provided by several different agencies.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Having similar issues handled by various agencies could slow down response time to feedback, especially when it is not clear which agency should be the one to follow up or if no agency steps up to take up the lead.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: One area that MSO could look into is the treatment of pest problems.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Pests as defined by the National Environment Agency (NEA) include rodents, mosquitoes and cockroaches while general wildlife handled by AVA includes crows and pigeons which can also become pests.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Bees or birds on roadside trees are referred to NParks while those on trees on state land are handled by HDB, and Town Councils will handle insect or bird complaints on trees in common properties of HDB.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Unlike grass and trees, rodents move, insects and birds fly.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Residents can complain to the Town Council about a pest problem, but the nest or source could be across the boundary in a non-Town Council area.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: In a compact environment where land boundaries of various agencies are in close proximity, having multiple agencies work together to manage a pest problem is not efficient and often not effective.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The current approach of handling such issues by referral to different agencies is based on land boundary.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: As such, many residents approach the Town Councils with feedback on municipal issues.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: It has been a year since the pilot started.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: These companies have pipes, cables and meters at HDB common corridors and residents tend to complain to the Town Council when something is amiss.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The Town Council refers the feedback accordingly to the respective companies but the tracking and closing of loops need to be better managed.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Would MSO be able to look into this by tapping on the existing system with public agencies?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: MSO's objective is to provide a convenient single point of contact for residents to make reports and coordinate multiple agencies or Ministries to help solve the problems at hand.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A famous writer once wrote: "What is essential is invisible to the eye".

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: They are often overlooked, like having a clean pavement to walk on or a damaged railing repaired promptly.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But these are essential things in our living environment.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It has been slightly over a year since MSO was formed to work with various agencies to improve these essential services.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is a good base to build on.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For feedback that involves multiple agencies, MSO is actively improving the work process.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: You may have read about the case concerning the cleanliness of waters around Marina Country Club earlier this year.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Litter accumulated on the waters and an adjoining temporary drain, making the area look unsightly.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: MSO brought together the relevant agencies – the Maritime and Port Authority (MPA), NEA, PUB, SLA – and facilitated a coordinated response.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: With SLA fronting the operations, the agencies cleaned the area and embarked on constructing a permanent drain.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The agencies also agreed on procedures to address future cases.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Alex Yam and Mr Chong Kee Hiong asked about our challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Improving response time to feedback is not our only goal.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have also been working to make it more convenient for the public to get to us on municipal issues.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: MSO launched the OneService app in January last year.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Several Members asked about the public response to the app.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Specifically, 5% of feedback was received via the OneService app.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: MSO and our partner agencies will continue to improve our digital channels.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have received suggestions on the app and introduced several enhancements.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These include adding new reporting categories and push notifications on the status of your cases.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Many Members wanted to know our upcoming plans.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This year, we will introduce a new crowdsourcing feature to collect information that helps our agencies to address municipal issues which users do not expect a reply.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will pilot crowdsourcing in the retrieval of abandoned supermarket trolleys.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I am sure many of us have encountered the odd supermarket trolley at void decks or walkways, which caused obstruction or was being used as a litter dump.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This feature will be available on the OneService App by the end of this month and it marks a milestone in extending our partnership beyond Government agencies to the private sector.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: When you next see an abandoned trolley, simply use the OneService App to submit its location.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will pump the data to the supermarkets which will go around to collect them periodically.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For residents, there will be fewer abandoned trolleys in the community; for supermarkets, they will be able to retrieve their trolleys more efficiently.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: If the "Spot Abandoned Trolleys" initiative works well, we will look at expanding crowdsourcing arrangements to other municipal issues.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Besides the OneService App, MSO will be introducing the OneService Web Portal in the latter half of this year.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This will be a one-stop platform that aggregates relevant information from our partner agencies that affects your neighbourhood, such as dengue clusters in your neighbourhood, HDB block-cleaning schedules in your precincts and traffic incidents in the surrounding areas.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: You can also report and track your feedback on either the app or Web Portal through the same account.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We hope our efforts will make it even easier for you to interact with Government agencies on issues relating to you and your neighbourhood.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Of course, residents can still submit feedback to agencies via existing channels.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong asked if MSO would look into improving processes and workflows.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: During the Budget debate, Dr Tan Wu Meng similarly called for better coordination on the ground.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Indeed, MSO will focus on improving the coordination between agencies in operations this year.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Having a lead agency as your point-of-contact helps us to ensure timely response to your feedback.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: AVA has been the first responder for animal-related issues since 2012.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As Mr Baey Yam Keng mentioned, MSO facilitated the centralisation of public greenery maintenance under NParks last year.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: NParks has been taking over the greenery maintenance functions in phases, starting with grass cutting.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Baey also asked that MSO look into other functions that cut across agencies to better streamline processes.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It means that if you see a damaged footpath or sheltered linkway and are unsure of whom to contact, you can use the OneService app, which will route such cases to LTA to assess and lead in the response.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As first responder, LTA will promptly attend to cases of public safety concerns to mitigate the risks.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For instance, LTA was recently alerted to a footpath damaged by tree roots in front of Hong Kah Secondary School.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: LTA immediately inspected the site and placed safety cones to warn pedestrians of the hazard.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: And together with NParks, both agencies worked together on the repair works.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For non-emergencies, LTA will also be a first point of contact and coordinate the issue, although the repair might be done by another agency.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As for other cross-cutting issues, including the issue of pest control mentioned by Mr Baey Yam Keng, given their complexity as well as the local context involved, we will accumulate experience and knowledge as we go through the cases, helping the agencies to solve local cases one by one.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will explore how to improve on the process and look at systemic improvement over time.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For instance, MSO co-created a manual with the pilot Town Councils and our agencies to clarify responsibilities for common municipal issues and facilitate prompt referrals.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is to ensure that residents' feedback will be promptly attended to, regardless of who they first approach.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Similar to our approach with the agencies, we have also moved beyond feedback management to collaborate on operations.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Several municipal issues require the Government and Town Councils to work closely together.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: One example is water leakage from pipe fittings in HDB blocks.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: When residents call PUB to report on a pipe leakage, often without a clear description of the location of the leak, PUB has to visit the site.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: If the leakage occurs within the segment of the pipe under the Town Council's care, PUB will temporarily stop the leak and refer the case to the Town Council for proper repair.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Two sets of technicians are often involved before the repair is done.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It leads to a delay in repair and wastage of labour.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To facilitate faster resolution, PUB and the pilot Town Councils tried a first responder protocol last year.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Under the protocol, they are assigned first responder roles for specified types of water supply issues.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: So, when a case on pipe leakage in Jurong East was reported to PUB in October last year, Jurong-Clementi Town Council attended to the feedback as the first responder for leaks in HDB estates and resolved it straightaway.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Similarly, MSO will look into improving the coordination between agencies and Town Councils for other issues like high-rise littering and pigeon feeding.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: However, our collaboration with Town Councils, as with other MSO initiatives, is not meant to and will not replace the functions of the Town Councils nor weaken their autonomy in service delivery.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: MSO and its partners are also leveraging technology and learning from each other to improve processes and productivity, which was what Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Mr Chong Kee Hiong and Mr Ong Teng Koon have asked about.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A good example is HDB, which used technology to manage their car park enforcement.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Instead of conducting time-consuming and manpower-intensive physical checks on the location of their wardens, HDB has enhanced the Electronic Handheld Terminals used by the wardens to capture their locations.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: HDB officers can now focus on car park management, such as addressing public feedback on illegal parking and obstruction of vehicles in car parks.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: SLA has been harnessing technology to improve the efficiency of their land surveys.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: They have now started using a software application called Oblivision, which allows officers to inspect and even measure structures on a particular plot of land, without physically going to the site.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: MSO has also commenced work with SLA to see how we can extend Oblivision to other agencies to reduce labour-intensive site visits.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: MSO is on a constant lookout for technologies that can help our agencies deliver better and more efficient services.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: There will not be major infrastructure built or goodies given out.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But through what we do, we constantly improve the essential services which define the quality of our living environment.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To do this, we will need to expand our network of partners, including private companies providing public services, like what Mr Baey asked for.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But most of all, we want to engage residents as our key stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Together, we can create a better living environment for one another and for the ones we love.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: To achieve this, we must establish higher productivity within the construction industry.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: What is the take-up rate of the Construction Productivity and Capability Fund (CPCF)?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: How useful has it been in encouraging greater innovation and productivity?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: What is the progress of adoption of new construction technologies, including Design for Manufacturing and Assembly through Prefabricated Pre-finished Volumetric Construction (PPVC)?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Do they bring about savings in manpower and shorten the construction period, as expected?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: At the same time, I was told that in Australia, PPVC is not so common.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: With proper planning, steel works can be faster than PPVC.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: So, I hope the Government does not over push PPVC and forget about other construction methods.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: CPCF mainly encourages firms to adopt more productive construction methods.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: A few Singaporean developers who ventured to Australia told me that, in Australia, they can build faster because they spend more effort and time in the design and planning stage.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: In Singapore, as the land cost is high, the developer would normally rush to have design and planning approval obtained so that they can launch quickly.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: As a result, a lot of details are not ironed out properly during the design and planning stage.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Tackling the downstream construction methods may not yield the results that we desire.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: We need to have fundamental changes in our workflow.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Besides giving more time for the upstream design and planning, we need to have experienced Singaporean Core engineers, architects and construction managers, that is, we need to retain and build on the construction expertise in Singapore to get better results.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: The Government can also help in procurement matters.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Do not automatically award the contracts to the lowest tenderer.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Instead, scrutinise the companies' local expertise too, and ask that they have a certain level of local expertise before they can get the contract.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Chairman, Sir, the construction industry is a very complex industry, comprising many stakeholders, such as the authorities, developers, consultants, suppliers, and contractors.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: With rising expectations from clients and users, construction projects are becoming more complex.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Thus, we need to find new ways to improve construction productivity and quality.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: First, what are the key initiatives implemented by the Ministry to improve the innovation, productivity, quality, safety and professionalism in the industry?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Two, what is the future roadmap for the construction industry?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: One, review the terms and conditions of all land sales and qualifying certificate for developers.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These cost increases are ultimately passed on to property buyers and users.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I propose that we review or remove these land sales requirements to allow more flexibility for developers to adopt more innovative and productive methods in their developments and encourage developers to be more creative in finding more cost-effective solutions for their developments.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Two, develop a fair remuneration framework for building consultants.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Today, building consultants, such as architects, engineers and quantity surveyors, are usually paid a percentage fee based on the value of the project.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Such a fee structure may result in a conflict of interest as some consultants may not be incentivised to produce simple, functional and lower-cost designs.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I urge the Ministry to consider developing a fair remuneration framework that will encourage building consultants to adopt professional practices and for a fair fee.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This could be in the form of lump-sum fees based on the size and complexity of the project.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Three, build a core team of Singapore builders.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many architecture, engineering and building professionals have left the industry.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is attributed to a lack of recognition of the professions, tough work environment and the poor image of the industry.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: At local universities, architecture, engineering and building courses are not top choices among university applicants.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I propose that the Ministry set up a Construction Future Steering Committee to make Singapore a Global City.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Many residents in Hougang welcome the new lifts although, for some elderly residents, it came too late.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: For others, the Lift Upgrading Programme (LUP) introduces a new set of problems and issues they never had to contend with before.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: For example, many would have thought that the installation of privacy louvres for the new LUP lift lobbies is a standard feature and a simple process as these are non-­structural installations.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: However, some privacy louvres serve no purpose whatsoever because the gaps between the fins are too wide.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some are not even angled correctly to achieve any effect.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In the same block of flats, some lift lobbies have louvres, and some do not.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The flow of water along the common corridors is also affected by LUP.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Water ponding and flooding became an issue for some residents as the original path of the water flow along the common corridor has been altered or re­routed.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: One major bugbear of LUP can be found at Block 314, Hougang Avenue 5.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Residents living at lift lobby C found out to their disappointment that a new 1.2-metre lift landing bridge was built right beside one of the two benefiting units on each floor without factoring in the proximity of the affected unit and the dry riser.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: While the new bridge may comply with the statutory requirements, the cement base of the dry riser effectively reduces the clear width of the entrance to less than 950 millimetres at the base level.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: With the landing valve of the dry riser sticking out substantially, the clear width of the entrance of the lift landing was further reduced at about the shoulder height level.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Taken as a whole, the lift landing bridge at Block 314 does not comply with the Singapore Civil Defence Force’s (SCDF) requirements as the entrance does not have the 1.2-metre clear width.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In the case of Block 314, the new lift landing bridge meets the requirements, but it is located right next to a dry riser and a resident's flat.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Affected residents can no longer leave their gates open or leave their shoes outside their doorway as that will also cause obstruction at the entrance of the lift landing.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: These residents do not even have any space left to put a simple shoe rack anymore.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The Town Council has no issue to enforce its by­law to ensure that these passageways are not being obstructed indiscriminately but we are looking at a situation where the design of the landing bridge is being forced upon the residents to such a point where anything left outside their units will cause obstruction, no matter what.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Is there any room for HDB to make good the bad designs as residents have to live with the consequences, day in and day out?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: And it does not help that LUP designs for similar flats in an estate can vary depending on the contractor who is doing the job.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I must stress that I am not talking about defects but design anomalies.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang, you have two cuts.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This is a relatively high breakdown rate, considering these new lifts are barely three years old.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I am not sure whether this happens only in Aljunied-Hougang Town or across the board.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Next, with the growth in the number of lifts contributed by LUP, the expenditure on lift maintenance for each year is also rising.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This gives rise to maintenance issues, as the original manufacturers control the parts and pricing.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I suggest HDB consider a standardised lift design for HDB estates to require manufacturers to produce lifts based on a standard design and make the standardised lift parts, so that both electronic and mechanical parts will be readily available.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This will ensure competitive pricing in the manufacture and maintenance of lifts.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In 2013, I filed a cut noting that a pilot project under the Greenprint Initiative was slated to be carried out in Jurong East in 2013 and 2014.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Such a system can afford all Town Councils not only better productivity but also savings in manpower costs.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It is environmentally sustainable and gets rid of the problem of foul smells during refuse collection.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In June 2015, HDB said it would test-bed this pneumatic system in Yuhua.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: What has been the Ministry's assessment of applying the system to an existing HDB estate?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Can the Ministry comment on how feasible it will be to roll out the system to other HDB estates, especially the older ones?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It appears that upcoming HDB projects at Tampines North, Bidadari and Punggol Northshore will also have the same system.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: However, the modernisation of waste collection is a benefit that should be experienced by as many HDB estates as possible, including the older HDB estates.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Many residents I have spoken to welcome this form of assistance rendered by HDB and it lessens their financial burden.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: However, concerns persist, and I would like to reflect my residents' sentiments in this House.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: For instance, if the ceiling at the lower floor unit faces a leak or has signs of leakage, such as distinct watermark or a blotted patch, no repair works would be done to the damaged ceiling.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: This is not fair to the lower floor home owners.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: As a Member who represents a mature estate, I have regularly received feedback on the wear and tear to the ceiling in the unit.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: In fact, a resident who is staying in the lower floor unit said to me that in order to make repairs to her unit, she had to fork out additional costs.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: She is of the view that the repair of this damaged ceiling and its consequent repair costs should be included in the GRA scheme as the damage of their unit's ceiling should be the joint responsibility of both owners in accordance with the spirit of this particular policy.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I am in agreement with her on this.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: The present policy has good intention, but we must be careful not to allow one set of family feeling shortchanged and left out.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, not many people know that there is a natural hot spring in Singapore, and it is located in Sembawang, off Gambas Avenue.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This Sembawang hot spring is our one and only natural hot spring on our island here.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The exact source of the hot spring remains unknown.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Hot springs are formed when under groundwater enters the earth's crust as deep as three kilometres underground and get heated up to high temperatures by the hot rock masses.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The high pressure causes the hot boiling water to seep upwards through cracks, thereby forcing itself out of the ground into a spring.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: At this point, the temperature of the water drops to about 70 degrees.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There is an interesting history to our hot spring.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In 1909, Seah Eng Keong, the son of Pioneer Seah Liang Seah, had discovered hot springs in his pineapple estate and channelled the springs all together so they could be concentrated in one area.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: A well was built along the spring and became popular with the villagers.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The village was then known as Kampong Ayer Panas, which means "Village of Hot Water".

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In 1922, soft drinks firm Fraser & Neave (F&N) acquired the site and set up a plant nearby to tap the hot mineral water, which it bottled and called "Seletaris".

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: During World War II, the Japanese forces, upon learning the existence of the hot spring, built a number of thermal baths, or onsen, in the area, to relax as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There is immense educational value for our students as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If the hot spring park is properly developed and promoted, I am confident that it will become a popular attraction for all of us to enjoy.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, the development of the Rail Corridor as an oasis and unique community space is an exciting one for many Singaporeans, especially to residents staying around that area.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Green areas, foot paths and bicycle paths, as well as surrounding developments along the Rail Corridor, are woven together seamlessly.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The old Bukit Timah Fire Station will be developed as an attraction and gateway node to the Rail Corridor.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The winning design has plans for the former Bukit Timah Fire Station to be a gateway to the Bukit Timah Nature Reserve.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Here, a forest walk and observation tower will let visitors get close to nature.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Residents staying at Hume, who live near the Bukit Timah Fire Station, are very keen to know about the developments of the Rail Corridor.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Increased human traffic to the area will be a key factor of consideration for the building of a Hume MRT station.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The opening of Downtown Line 2 has brought much convenience and easy commute to many Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, Hume residents presently continue to look longingly from the outside, as the line passes through their area without a stop.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: New land sites for housing can enhance the liveability factor along the Railway Corridor and enhance its unique proposition of a residential and community oasis.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As implementation on various stretches of the corridor is being studied carefully and paced accordingly, we hope MND will give this serious consideration as plans for the Railway Corridor continue to be shaped and refined in response to public feedback.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Chairman, several existing businesses would like to continue their trade in the same area rather than moving to a new location.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: However, in mature neighbourhood centres, many of their remaining leases are 10 years or less.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Business operators and residents share strong sentiment of the place and businesses were their "go-to" shops in the neighbourhood.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Co-funding for the scheme and rent-free period during renovation do not resolve their concerns over the lease period.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: For shops that were previously sold, many would have been sublet to tenants.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: This usually results in frequent change of tenants.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The shop owners also have no keen interest to be part of the ROS scheme as maximising rental is their primary aim.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: We often end up with a poor mix of business types, having multiple tenants within same vicinity conducting similar businesses.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: This creates competition but yet a lack of diversity in offerings.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: In this regard, since the Government is encouraging startups, it should consider and assist those with innovative business models or those revitalising traditional trades by offering shop spaces in the neighbourhood over a shorter lease period.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: This helps to reduce their startup cost, serves as an incubation bed for potentials and inject new elements to the mature estates, at least a different variety from the retail chain stores that are common in our malls today.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: I believe that rejuvenation of our heartlands is just as important, if not more than infrastructural changes or beautifying and modernising the landscape.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: We also need to ensure that we have a right mix of businesses and encourage startups or social businesses to form an ecosystem in our neighbourhood and town centres.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Mr Chairman, enhancing the Revitalisation of Shops (ROS) scheme and the just announced Favourite Place initiative, serve up an excellent opportunity for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in the neighbourhood to strive towards their full potential.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Heartland businesses play a major role in job creation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: They also make the estates a livelier place to live in.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Moreover, they provide residents with services and products with the added benefit of convenience of access, and I believe usually at greater affordability than the shops in the shopping malls.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Can the Minister or MND kindly give an update on the progress of the ROS scheme for shops in the heartland?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: How many estates have undergone revitalisation and which estates are next in the pipeline?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Has the range of services and products offered at these revitalised shops expanded as a result of the upgrading programmes?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But of course, this has to be weighed against the higher traffic during that period.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, the selection of the heartland shops or the shop location is important to boost the activity.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: (In Mandarin):   We have high hopes for the Enhanced ROS scheme announced by the Finance Minister.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: During the Budget debate last year, I highlighted two shortcomings of the current ROS scheme to the Ministry of National Development (MND).

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: These are the main reasons why only a few neighbourhood shop precincts have been successfully upgraded.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Although we have merchant associations to bring the heartland shops together, not all act in unison.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Very often, there will be one or two shops that are less cooperative, especially for shop owners who lease the shops to other tenants.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: They are basically investors who are more concerned about rental income than neighbourhood upgrading.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: As a result, the upgrading programme cannot proceed because of them.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Thus, I hope the Minister can take into consideration the interest of the majority of the shop owners and patrons and adopt the model for Home Improvement Programme (HIP) on the use of polling.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: However, Government grants for upgrading have remained the same.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: As a result, the ROS scheme has become increasingly unattractive.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In response to my plea last year in Parliament, MND agreed to set up a new Revitalise Heartland Shops Committee, chaired by then Senior Minister of State Mr Lee Yi Shyan, to review and refine the ROS scheme.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I was invited to join the committee and had several meetings with shop owners, grassroots organisations and HDB.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: We have received a lot of valuable feedback but there was no conclusive decision.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: So, I hope the Minister can give our shop owners a reply in Parliament today.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Chairman, many of our private estates are at least 30 years old with many elderly residents.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: New widened footpaths with ramps will be welcomed by wheelchair or stroller users.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Public playgrounds and exercise areas may need renovation so that they remain safe for users.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Minister Lawrence Wong earlier described how newer HDB towns, such as Bidadari, Tampines North and Tengah, will be better designed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: At the same time, we have been Remaking Our Heartland under a programme started in 2007 with that name, to rejuvenate and transform our older estates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: At Dawson Estate in Queenstown, one of our oldest HDB towns, new public housing is set within a park environment, but heritage elements of old Dawson are being preserved.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, the former wet market at Block 38 Commonwealth Avenue has been conserved and will be refurbished to house retail shops.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Over in Yishun, residents can look forward to a new integrated development comprising shops, an air-conditioned bus interchange, a community club and town plaza, all of which will add greater buzz to the town centre.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In Bedok, with the Outdoor Play Corridor, residents and park users will be able to cycle seamlessly from East Coast Park, through the Bedok Town Centre, all the way to Bedok Reservoir by next year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If you have been to Jurong East recently, you would have seen the transformation of the Jurong Gateway area, with the opening of commercial malls next to the MRT station, and two hospitals, Ng Teng Fong Hospital and Jurong Community Hospital.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Jurong Lake Gardens West, part of our third National Gardens, will also be completed in two years' time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Miss Cheryl Chan suggested that agencies involve local communities more during town design, especially for mature towns.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Last year, we shared our plans to rejuvenate Woodlands, Pasir Ris and Toa Payoh under the Remaking Our Heartland 3 programme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Over the course of one year, HDB connected with some 400 residents and local stakeholders in these towns to consult them on preliminary concepts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some residents from Woodlands hoped that their town remains green and asked for a larger community space within Woodlands Central.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Pasir Ris residents requested for a rejuvenated town centre and for the existing parks and commercial spaces to be upgraded.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Toa Payoh residents desired a balance between older and newer developments, and for a greener and even more senior-friendly environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: HDB has been refining the proposals based on these ideas and suggestions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The preliminary proposals are exciting, and cover three broad themes, namely, Identity, Public Spaces and Connectivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For Woodlands Town, residents can look forward to a transformed Woodlands Waterfront with interesting landscaping.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In addition, within Woodlands Central, there will be a town plaza, which will offer a sizeable space for various large-scale activities, including those for the community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For Pasir Ris, we plan to introduce a mixed-use development integrated with a new bus interchange in the town centre and upgrade the parks in the town.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In Toa Payoh, we are looking to revamp the pedestrian mall in Toa Payoh Town Centre with more greenery, rest areas and covered shopping streets at selected stretches for residents to enjoy, even when it rains.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will also introduce dedicated cycling paths throughout the town to improve connectivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Since 2007, the scheme has benefited about half of all HDB shops in town and neighbourhood centres, with upgraded shop fronts and funding support for business promotional activities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Last year, we announced that we would revise or review the ROS scheme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: HDB shops play an important role in building our heartland communities and we want to support them better.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As Mr Saktiandi Supaat said, they make our estates a much livelier place to live in.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They are where we buy our daily necessities and groceries, get our nasi lemak, chicken rice or kopi-o.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The shopkeepers in our heartlands are often familiar faces that we grow up with.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In carrying out the review, we consulted the heartland retail community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We set up the Revitalisation of Heartland Shops Committee comprising representatives from various merchants associations, retailers and grassroots organisations, to tap on their experience.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We also conducted focus group discussions with merchants associations across the island, to hear their views.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have evaluated the suggestions carefully, and this is what we plan to do.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: HDB will announce the details before launching the next batch of ROS soon.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our review is still continuing and there may be more in the pipeline.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng makes a valid point that one of the challenges preventing a higher take-up of ROS upgrading is the need for unanimous or near unanimous support from shopkeepers or shop owners before upgrading works can commence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: One possible solution is to set a threshold so that a certain percentage of shop owners polled want ROS upgrading, then this binds all the shops in the neighbourhood centre.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On the other hand, some retailers have also shared that upgrading works are less useful to them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Miss Cheryl Chan said we should ensure a right mix of businesses in the heartlands and asked whether SMEs and startups can be encouraged to set up shops there.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, we are already seeing a trend of an increasing number of young entrepreneurs setting up shops in the heartlands, such as ice cream parlours, artisan bakeries and hipster cafes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Not only do we have an extensive network of parks and park connectors, we have also incorporated greenery wherever we can, from walls to rooftops, to make it pervasive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, we will make our parks more community centric.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In the next few years, we will continue to roll out inclusive playgrounds in our parks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They enable all kids to have fun together, whether they are physically able or have disabilities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The first was launched last year at Bishan-Ang Mo Kio Park, with the support of the National Council of Social Services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will also use greenery as therapy, especially for seniors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A study conducted by NParks and the National University Health System (NUHS) showed improved mental health in participants who participated in "horticultural therapy".

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, with rapid urbanisation, we recognise that Singaporeans are also concerned about green spaces rich in our cultural and natural heritage.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Low Yen Ling had asked about URA's plans for the development of the old Bukit Timah Fire Station as a key attraction and gateway to the Rail Corridor.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Indeed, the winning proposal for URA's Request for Proposals last year shows how we can sensitively adapt the former Bukit Timah Fire Station as a hub for nature activities, providing seamless access to the nearby nature parks and the Bukit Timah Nature Reserve.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As we implement these plans, we want to involve people who live, work and play along the Corridor, and create opportunities for them to lead community-based initiatives along the Rail Corridor.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is why URA recently embarked on an unprecedented effort to consult residents along the Rail Corridor, from Tanjong Pagar Railway Station in the south to Kranji in the north, through a series of local exhibitions and dedicated workshops.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Residents told us about the types of trails and landscapes they wanted to see and how to retain its rustic character while making improvements so that it can be enjoyed by all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Many workshop participants also tried their hand at master planning, drawing out their own ideas for each area.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, different residents with different interests had to debate, discuss with one another and then decide what to put where, what to have and what not to have.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak asked if it can be developed into a park.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As he rightly pointed out, the springs have an interesting history and are currently on the Ministry of Defence's (MINDEF) land.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are studying if we can sensitively enhance the area, in line with existing natural features, heritage and land use.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Where possible, we want to retain and enhance such places, with the community, for everyone to enjoy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Beyond creating new green spaces with the community, we also want to support ground-up greening efforts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Today, we have about 1,000 Community in Bloom (CIB) gardens and 20,000 community gardeners.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some of these gardeners have gone the extra mile, contributing their harvests to disadvantaged families in the neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Others use the gardens as an outdoor classroom to teach the younger generation about nature and how life used to be in the past, passing down knowledge and values along the way.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The CIB programme is no longer just about spreading the love of gardening, but also the spirit of neighbourliness.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They are about how communities come together to generate a greater social good.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have seen organic communities form at other parks, too, such as brisk-walkers, joggers, exercise groups, cyclists, nature lovers, heritage buffs, educators and so on.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That is why NParks launched the Friends of the Park scheme two weeks ago.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Through this, volunteers can be even more involved in our parks, for example, by organising their own activities and partnering NParks in park management.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are happy to have some of our long-time volunteers step up to lead these communities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, Mr Sivasothi will chair the community for the Friends of Chestnut Nature Park, which we just opened.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Well-known in the nature fraternity, he has been volunteering for over 20 years, conducting coastal clean-ups and nature walks, and is also an avid cyclist.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Over time, I believe we will see more people like him coming forward to jointly create and sustain a green and liveable environment for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Coming to the third plank of my speech, Sir, this spirit of partnership, which I spoke about earlier, to rejuvenate our heartlands and enhance our green spaces also extends to our ongoing efforts to transform our built environment sector and how we will build our city of the future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Over the years, we have progressively raised the professionalism, safety and quality in the sector through initiatives, such as licensing builders, regulating buildability and raising workmanship quality through CONQUAS and Quality Mark.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: From 2010, we have also put in significant effort and resources to raise construction productivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The transformation that we are seeking is slowly taking shape.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The level of prefabrication for building structural systems and wall systems has increased significantly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Safety and quality will also be enhanced with more prefabrication.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While this is positive, we should make a big push for even higher productivity gains over the next five years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our vision of the future built environment sector is one that is efficient and collaborative, where industry stakeholders jointly go through the design and construction of a project in virtual reality first to finalise details and minimise abortive works.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The building components are then manufactured and prefinished offsite in factories and then transported onsite for clean and quiet assembly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Meanwhile, autonomous drones are used to complete other tasks concurrently.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our built environment sector of the future will be one that is highly advanced, highly skilled and highly integrated.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Buildings will be constructed faster with higher quality and lower impact on the surrounding neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As both Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Dr Teo Ho Pin have rightly pointed out, the Government has to very closely partner the industry and the entire ecosystem, if we are to effectively change the way we build, because there are different industry players involved in every project – developers, consultants, architects, contractors, sub-contractors – and there are many moving pieces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Jobs will have to be redesigned, and processes will have to evolve or change, as part of the transformation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Critically, there needs to be more collaboration among key stakeholders upstream, as Er Dr Lee Bee Wah quite rightly pointed out.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Everyone has to play our part and be prepared to break out of our comfort zones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To date, we have seen a handful of projects in the public and private sectors adopting the Design for Manufacturing and Assembly (DfMA) approach and embracing game-changing technology.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Nanyang Technological University’s (NTU) North Hill Hostel and OUE's Crowne Plaza Extension were the first projects to adopt Prefabricated Prefinished Volumetric Construction (PPVC) in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Such projects can be built quite quickly, with less disamenity to people living and working in the surroundings because the modules, the entire rooms, so to speak, are prefabricated, sometimes with all finishes and fittings complete, before being brought onto the site for installation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But besides PPVC, there are many other productive technologies on the DFMA spectrum that the industry can adopt, as Er Dr Lee Bee Wah mentioned.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These include advanced precast, structural steel and cross-laminated timber (CLT), which can bring about productivity gains and a reduction in manpower, as compared to traditional methods.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: At the same time, we recognise that there are challenges.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Workforce upgrading, regulatory hurdles and logistics issues are some of the teething problems that the early adopters have faced.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We value the industry's feedback and will do what we can to help the industry quickly overcome this learning curve.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, let me share some of the work in progress.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: BCA has also formulated a Sectoral Manpower Plan to ensure that future manpower demand can be met.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: With the support of our firms, we will continue to attract, retain and upgrade our workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, companies can partner BCA in its suite of scholarship and sponsorship programmes which aims to bring in new Singaporean entrants to the built environment sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Further, through our Earn and Learn Programmes under SkillsFuture, our diploma and ITE graduates can continue learning while working, through on-the-job training, mentorship and upgrading courses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: BCA also works closely with the industry associations, such as the Singapore Contractors Association Limited (SCAL), to conduct regular Productivity Clinics since 2011.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: About 350 companies have benefited from these one-on-one sessions with BCA as they embarked on their productivity journey.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To encourage the wider adoption of DfMA and Virtual Design and Construction (VDC) and smoothen their implementation, we have taken the lessons learnt from the early adopters and set up a taskforce to look at building up an ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Dr Teo Ho Pin spoke earlier about having a whole-of-ecosystem steering committee.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Here, we have set up a task force to drive the entire ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The industry will be consulted on its recommendations as part of the process.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have also reviewed regulatory requirements where necessary.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To facilitate optimal design for prefabrication and modularisation, LTA is reviewing requirements for the escort of oversized loads being transported, without compromising road safety.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are also considering setting aside land for PPVC production in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To fast track the regulatory approval process for innovative technologies new to Singapore, we have set up the multi-agency Building Innovation Panel since 2011.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For the long term, we are scanning the horizon for potential technologies and new ideas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Promising areas include 3-D printing, robotics, infocomm technology (ICT) and data analytics in the built environment sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The roadmap will help guide our R&D efforts for the sector and can provide valuable insights to the Committee on the Future Economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Just like how prefabrication and precast have now become prevalent, we can expect DfMA and VDC to become the norm in future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: With the public sector leading the way and closely partnering the industry, I am confident that our vision of a highly integrated, advanced and skilled built environment sector is achievable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On the Lift Upgrading Programme (LUP), Mr Png Eng Huat had mentioned some concerns at Block 314.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Please raise it to HDB or to MND so that we can have a better look at it.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang spoke about lift maintenance, lift parts and lift breakdowns.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On the point on lift breakdowns, there is a tele-monitoring system in every lift in HDB, which provides data remotely to the Town Council, so you can establish what the cause of the fault is.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, I would urge the hon Member to take a look at the Town Council data and have a sense as to what the causes of these frequent breakdowns are.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some of it could be the nature of the use of the lift, some of it could be the frequency of the Town Council's maintenance regime or the capability and competence of the engineers they engage, among other reasons.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, I think it is good to drill down and analyse what your problems are.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As for the cost of maintenance which Mr Low Thia Khiang said is high because some original parts are owned by the lift manufacturer, this is something that will depend on the complexity of the part.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There are over 20 lift brands used in HDB estates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, there are a variety of parts, from smaller parts, simpler parts that can be manufactured by others to those that are more specialised and specific to the lift.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang also talked about the high cost of lift maintenance and replacement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MND is reviewing ways to help Town Councils better manage the lifts and to plan ahead for the lift replacement needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Given that lift replacement is a major sinking fund expenditure, Town Councils should monitor their long-term financial sufficiency.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Even so, my Ministry has provided Town Councils with additional assistance schemes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang has also asked about the outcomes of the Greenprint programme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: HDB launched the first two HDB Greenprint projects at Yuhua in 2012 and Teck Ghee in 2015 respectively to introduce sustainable living concepts into existing HDB estates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Yuhua project was just completed last November and we are still assessing the effectiveness of the project, the various components of the project, including the Pneumatic Waste System that Mr Low talked about.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Based on HDB's preliminary survey, Yuhua residents welcome the green features, including the secured bicycle parking and hobby farming zones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It may be more challenging to do so in existing older estates, due to site constraints and higher costs, but we will assess the performance of the system at Yuhua first before deciding on the next step.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I listened to what the Member said and I think it will be better if he raises the specific cases to us, for us to be better able to assess what the problem is.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Working with diverse stakeholders, especially those with conflicting viewpoints, may not be the fastest way of getting things done, but it is necessary if we are to ensure that we, as Singaporeans, take ownership of the kind of Singapore we want for ourselves and our children, that we hear and understand the differences in views from the diversity of interests making up our plural society and respect the choices then made to create not only a liveable environment but also a sustainable one.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I believe the process of engagement, collaboration and joint stewardship can bring us closer together as a national community, as a plural but cohesive nation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This must be the foundation upon which a better, brighter future will be built in the decades to come.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Chairman, Sir, as Singapore rapidly urbanised, new blocks and offices mushroomed, while farms were almost completely weeded out.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: With agricultural land relatively scarce today, the farm-trepreneur needs to be prudent to ensure that their investment pays off.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: While APF is committed to driving up productivity, perhaps the key factor driving down adoption is the short tenancies, coupled with the longer time it takes for farm owners or farm operators to recover investments, and double coupled by the uncertainty of land acquisition.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: They currently have a basic 10-year lease with another uncertain 10, only if there are no other developmental uses for the land.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: As such, I urge the Ministry to consider providing for the flexibility of 15-year leases, which is half that of industrial leases.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: At the current moment, we import nearly 90% of our food produce and food security dictates that we continue to increase local productivity, innovate through mechanisation, and maximise land usage for better yields.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: We need to transform our local farming industry to make it a strong productive pillar of our economic defence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: AVA currently devotes significant resources into hiring for-profit companies to manage stray dogs, cats and wild monkeys.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: AVA is working with animal welfare groups (AWGs) to rehome the dogs and cats that were impounded but this does not address the root of the problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: AVA currently does not partner any AWGs to manage the monkey issues.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Will AVA consider working more closely with and divert funding from the for-profit companies to the non-profit AWGs who are struggling to find funding and were already on the ground and helping to manage these issues?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This is a win-win solution that will address both public safety and animal welfare concerns and result in a more humane and long-term approach.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It might also result in cost savings for AVA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: With increased awareness on animal welfare, we can expect more reports from members of the public who are now more vigilant and concerned about this issue.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This will result in an increased workload for AVA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can the Ministry clarify whether it has sufficient resources and manpower to respond in a timely manner and rapidly to such cases?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In addition, wildlife trafficking has been added into the list of transnational organised crimes in ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Wildlife trafficking pushes species towards extinction and also destroys the habitat these animals live in.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: There are now also reports of how wildlife trafficking funds the activities of some terrorist groups.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In the past decade, there have already been several high-profile cases of wildlife trafficking in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can the Ministry elaborate on its plans to tackle wildlife trafficking and similarly, clarify whether it has sufficient resources and manpower to respond in a timely manner and rapidly to such cases?

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Chairman, thank you for allowing me to speak.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In his speech, Minister Lawrence Wong quoted from our iconic national song "Home", which says: "There is comfort in the knowledge, that home's about its people too".

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For households who have fallen onto hard times, the Government helps them in various ways.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: One of these is enabling them to stay in heavily subsidised public rental flats.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For those in urgent need of rental housing or any housing, HDB may give them priority allocation for a rental flat or provide them with Interim Rental Housing while they await their rental flat.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The increase in rental flats is not only about the increase in quantity.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We build rental flats in more locations with a better geographical spread and we integrate them within estates by locating them together with home ownership flats.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These efforts help to promote interaction among residents, as Mr Chong Kee Hiong has called for, and ensure that tenants have the same access to amenities that people staying in home ownership flats enjoy.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With rental flats in more locations, it is also more likely that tenants can get a flat nearer the preferred location of their choice.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: However, we should not increase our rental supply indefinitely.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Staying in public rental flats should only be temporary for families to rebuild their lives.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew said, "My primary preoccupation was to give every citizen a stake in the country and its future.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We want to see families in rental flats progress into homeownership.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Thus, we provide substantial help, such as generous housing grants of up to $80,000 for first-timer families.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about the supply of 2-room flats to help our rental families to buy a flat.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We currently set aside 10% of 2- and 3-room flats in our sales exercises under the Tenants' Priority Scheme (TPS).

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is 8.5 times more than the 48 applications we received that year.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These second-timer families in rental flats have the same housing need as first-timer rental families.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But as second timers, they have a lower allocation quota when it comes to balloting for new HDB flats.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Taken together, the Fresh Start Housing Scheme and the extension of TPS to second-timer rental families are significant measures to help our rental families achieve homeownership again and to build a more inclusive society.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For those in mortgage arrears, our primary objective is to help them retain their flats.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: HDB proactively engages households on how to resolve their HDB mortgage issues, especially those with loan arrears.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For example, HDB may temporarily reduce or defer their mortgage instalments to help their cash flow situation.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For those who need more long-term solutions, HDB may help them right-size to a more affordable flat with another HDB concessionary loan if necessary.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We also take a needs-based approach in assessing applications for a rental flat.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: If an applicant is assessed to have low income, no other affordable housing options and no family support; in other words, those who are at extremely high risk of having no roof over their heads, HDB will help them.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Even if the applicant does not fulfil some of the eligibility criteria, HDB will exercise flexibility based on their individual circumstances.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Together with other agencies and social workers, HDB will hold joint case conferences to find the best way to help them.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As Mr Faisal Manap said earlier, many of these families have multifaceted and multifactorial, complex issues.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
